Boris Cherny is a staff engineer at Anthropic. He shared his personal CLAUDE.md, the rules Claude Code follows every session automatically.

Here is what makes it different from what most people write.

Plan first. Write the plan before touching any code. If something goes wrong mid-task, stop and re-plan. Never push through.

Subagents. Offload complex work, keep the main context clean, throw more compute at hard problems.

Self-improvement loop. Every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md. Next session reads it and applies it. Mistake rate drops over time.

Verification standard. Never mark a task complete without proving it works. Run tests, check logs. Ask yourself: would a staff engineer approve this?

Demand elegance. For non-trivial changes, pause and ask if there is a more elegant solution. If a fix feels hacky, rebuild it properly.

Autonomous bug fixing. When given a bug, just fix it. Go to the logs, find the root cause, resolve it.

Git discipline. Commit at logical checkpoints. Never push to main without confirming the branch.

Most people treat CLAUDE.md as notes. Boris treats it as a contract. Claude Code is held to these standards every session automatically.

DVndfhOE7A9.caption:
A single shepherd dog can control an entire flock of sheep without ever touching them. The secret is spatial pressure — the exploitation of every prey animal's flight zone.
When a predator (or herding dog) enters the flight zone — the minimum distance at which an animal perceives a threat — the animal moves away. The dog does not chase individual sheep. Instead, it positions itself behind the flock relative to the target destination. This creates a directional pressure wave that pushes the entire group forward.
The pressure force follows an inverse-distance relationship: F = (1 − d/R)^1.2, where R is the pressure radius. Sheep closer to the dog flee harder. Sheep at the edge barely react. This gradient is what gives the dog fine control over the flock's direction.
The sheep themselves follow boids rules — three local interaction forces that produce emergent flocking:
Cohesion: steer toward the average position of nearby neighbors
Alignment: match heading with neighbors
Separation: avoid crowding
When the dog's pressure disrupts this equilibrium, the flock compresses, redirects, and flows toward the pen. Stubborn sheep dampen their flee response, requiring the dog to close distance and work harder. Low cohesion scatters the flock, forcing the dog to repeatedly round up stragglers.
Real shepherd dogs like Border Collies instinctively use these pressure mechanics. They arc behind the flock, oscillate side to side, and apply graduated pressure — behaviors directly modeled in this simulation.

DVCBNQ8jCly.caption:
How does a brainless colony find the shortest path through a maze without a map or a leader? The answer lies in a phenomenon called Stigmergy—a form of decentralized coordination where individuals interact through chemical modifications to their environment.
This simulation brings Ant Colony Optimization (ACO) to life, modeling the precise feedback loops that govern swarm intelligence. Each autonomous agent manages two distinct data streams: a Home Trail and a Food Trail. As ants navigate between their nest and a resource, they deposit volatile pheromones. Because ants on a shorter path complete their round-trips faster, they reinforce their route with more pheromone per unit of time compared to those on longer detours. This creates a Positive Feedback Loop, rapidly recruiting the rest of the colony to the most efficient trajectory.
The underlying mechanics are governed by a discrete approximation of the Diffusion-Evaporation Equation: ∂τ/∂t = Δτ + D∇²τ - ρτ. This equation balances three critical factors: the recruitment of new trail (Δτ), the spatial spread of information via diffusion (D), and the pruning of weak or obsolete data through exponential decay (ρ). By adjusting the Exploration-Exploitation tradeoff, we can observe the colony transition from chaotic discovery to laser-focused optimization.
This isn't just a biological curiosity; these exact principles power the modern world. From packet switching in telecommunications and vehicle routing in logistics to the way artificial neural networks search for global minima, the "Ant Logic" remains a gold standard for solving high-complexity, non-linear routing problems.
Key Technical Concepts:
Stigmergy: Environment-mediated coordination among autonomous agents.
Bi-directional Navigation: Using dual chemical fields to orient toward different goals.
Positive Feedback: Self-reinforcing signals that amplify efficient behaviors.
Stochastic Steering: Probabilistic movement based on local gradient sensing.

The wall-to-wall coverage of the Strait of Hormuz has been consistent: it’s closed, and the world is on the brink of catastrophe.

Because on the ground, the reality looks very different.

In some cases, they’re even rerouting—but they’re still getting through. Notably, a number of Chinese vessels continue to pass.

So why does the global narrative lack this nuance?

Because much of modern reporting relies on a single system: AIS (Automatic Identification System) data. And here’s the problem: there’s an entire “shadow fleet” of ships that either go dark or spoof their locations. Thousands of vessels operating outside that visibility.

So if your lens is AIS… you’re only seeing part of the picture.

And this points to something bigger.

In the name of efficiency, we’re increasingly outsourcing our understanding of the world to single data sources, centralized narratives, and now, even AI systems.

But truth is often less efficient.

It requires friction. It requires verification. Sometimes, it requires going there yourself.

Part of this is the application of the 60:30:10 color rule, a golden standard in design and art which breaks the frame into a dominant color (60%), a secondary color (30%) and an accent color (10%). Here, the rule is generally applied to beautiful, vast wide shots of landscapes, visualizing the scale of Jack’s journey in a manner pleasing to the eye.

This immersive art experience is intended to show how everything on Earth is connected - including us - and space makes that connection visible. 

Satellites track photosynthesis by measuring solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF), which is a faint glow emitted by plants that indicates the rate of carbon dioxide intake. Combined with other metrics like the “Greenness Index”, which uses near-infrared remote sensing to measure the amount of chlorophyll in plants, research teams from NASA, NOAA, JPL, Caltech, and more are uncovering new insight into our beautiful planet. Relevant data can be measured from satellites like the Japanese Greenhouse Gases Observing Satellite (GOSAT) and NASA’s Orbiting Carbon Observatory (OCO-1, 2, and 3), PACE, Sentinel, and other NOAA weather satellites.

Updated caption: for art inquiries please email hi@KimRoseArt.com 

—————-

The concept behind this piece sparked the theme of my upcoming solo show. Most of my ideas have been written down in my journal. That is where I like to brainstorm and see how I can push creative boundaries. Very few ideas have made my heart race, made me sweat, and this one in particular, made me crawl up into a ball. Lately, the ideas that scare me a bit have been hard to get out of my head. Later journaling what it meant to me, I cried. I still think this piece can make me cry if I sit and think about it too deeply. 

It was a strong reaction, I had to create the piece I wrote about. 

I have always hated blood. (If you made a face reading that don’t worry I made the same face originally, bear with me). Growing up my mom said I had such a steady hand, I should be a surgeon. I would always laugh and know I couldn’t ever consider it because the thought of blood alone makes my skin crawl. But I couldn’t think of anything more precious and life-giving than blood. How it represents life and death all together. How powerful it would be to create with. 

Three of the NFTs in my show were created with a mixture of my blood and poison. The mixture created some of the most beautiful movements I had ever seen. Something I once thought of as horrifying now became mesmerizing. It moved very differently from the paints and inks I’ve used before. It felt more alive. 

As these NFTs age, they get slower and darker. They then go black and die at the end of 100 years. After that, they glow gold for 9 months and then are reborn. We most likely won’t see this part, but our surviving generation will. 

These, as well as many other new NFTs and a few physical pieces, will be on display for my solo show in New York at @elsewhereart_ - they are also available, link in bio to purchase.

DXcDsyRCfdj.creator: adam_rosler
DXcDsyRCfdj.caption:
Same tokens. Different order. Different answer. Something inside the model is tracking position — and it’s not what most explainers tell you.

Attention is a dot product between a query vector and a key vector. A plain dot product doesn’t know which token came first. The fix is Rotary Position Embedding (RoPE): before the dot product, both vectors get rotated by an angle proportional to their position. Token one, a small rotation. Token fifty, a much bigger one.

Now the dot product depends on the difference between two positions. That difference IS the model’s sense of order. Llama, GPT, Gemini, Claude, DeepSeek — every attention head in every layer rotates vectors before comparing them.

Position is encoded as rotation, not addition. That’s how your model knows what comes before what.

DXUqQ7LiRNP.creator: adam_rosler
DXUqQ7LiRNP.caption:
Every token you send to an LLM leaves a trail. The model stores a key and a value vector per token, in full precision. That’s the KV cache. At 32k tokens on Llama 70B, it’s 17 gigabytes of GPU memory per request, and it only grows.

Engineers have been quantizing the cache down for years. 8 bits works. 4 bits mostly works. 3 bits always broke accuracy — until Google’s TurboQuant, accepted at ICLR 2026.

The trick: rewrite each vector in polar form. The angle distribution is known, so you only keep the radius and a few bits of angle. That’s PolarQuant. A Johnson-Lindenstrauss random rotation collapses the rest to sign bits.

Result: 3 bits per number instead of 16. Roughly 5x less memory. No finetuning, no calibration data, drops into any transformer. Long context for the price of short context.

In the summer of 2023, Ilya Sutskever, chief scientist at OpenAI and one of the key architects behind ChatGPT, found himself in a paradoxical moment. The technology he helped build had just become the fastest growing consumer product in history and pushed OpenAI’s valuation to tens of billions of dollars. Yet while the world celebrated the breakthrough, Sutskever quietly reviewed plans for a bunker, a reflection of his concern that artificial intelligence might one day become uncontrollable.

The origins of this moment trace back decades earlier to Geoffrey Hinton, the researcher who championed neural networks when most of the field believed the idea was impractical. In the 1970s and 1980s, the dominant approach to artificial intelligence focused on symbolic reasoning, where machines followed explicit rules and logic. Neural networks, designed to mimic how the brain learns patterns from data, struggled to gain acceptance and nearly disappeared due to lack of funding.

When a young Sutskever joined Hinton’s lab at the University of Toronto, the two researchers helped revive the field. Their work showed that larger neural networks trained with massive computing power could recognize patterns in images and language far better than earlier systems. That breakthrough helped ignite the modern AI era and eventually led to powerful models like GPT and applications such as ChatGPT.

Yet the same progress that made artificial intelligence so powerful also raised deeper concerns. Researchers who once struggled to make machines learn now face a more complex question. What happens if those machines become too capable? For pioneers like Sutskever and Hinton, the success of artificial intelligence carries a quiet realization that humanity may be building systems it does not yet fully understand.

There are five numbers that decide what your work is actually worth. Most artists guess all five, then blame the market.

Two. Your cost floor. Materials, framing, and the commission a gallery takes, often half. Clear it or you are paying to give the work away.

Pricing is not a feeling you have on the day. It is five numbers you work out once and hold.

🔧 4 GitHub repos to explore instead of scrolling ↓↓

Save this post for later!

⚙️ FREECAD — github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD
What it is: A fully open source parametric 3D CAD tool built for mechanical engineering
What you’ll find: The actual source code behind a professional grade CAD application — geometry kernels, constraint solvers, FEA integration, the lot
Why pull it apart: Reading how a real CAD tool is built teaches you more about design intent and parametric modelling than any tutorial ever will. Free to download and use right now.

🌊 OPENFOAM — github.com/OpenFOAM
What it is: The industry standard open source CFD simulation engine used by aerospace, automotive and energy companies worldwide
What you’ll find: Fluid dynamics solvers, mesh tools and simulation cases you can run on your own machine
Why pull it apart: Every time you design something that moves through air or fluid this is what the professionals use to validate it. Pull a tutorial case apart and run it. You will understand flow, pressure and heat transfer in a completely different way.

🤖 LEROBOT — github.com/huggingface/lerobot
What it is: Hugging Face’s open source robotics framework — hardware files, firmware, AI training tools all in one repo
What you’ll find: Full design files for the SO-101 robot arm, reinforcement learning and imitation learning code, datasets and pre-trained models
Why pull it apart: This is the most accessible on-ramp into AI controlled physical hardware available right now. Print the arm, run the code, train it to pick something up. The entire stack is open source.

🚁 JPL OPEN SOURCE ROVER — github.com/nasa-jpl/open-source-rover
What it is: NASA’s open source scaled down version of the Mars rover — designed entirely from consumer off the shelf parts
What you’ll find: Full mechanical design files, electronics schematics, firmware and build documentation
Why pull it apart: NASA built this specifically for people who want to learn mechanical engineering, electronics and software through a real build. If it is good enough for JPL it is good enough to learn from.

There Is No Democracy Without Journalism

Scott Pelley was asked about President Trump reportedly calling him a “stiff” and suggesting he was among people who “don’t care about the country.”

His response wasn’t about politics.

It was about service.

Pelley pointed to years spent covering wars alongside American troops in Iraq, Afghanistan, and Kuwait before making a broader point:

“There is no democracy without journalism. It can’t be done.”

Whether you agree with a journalist’s reporting or not, a free press is one of the institutions that allows citizens to hold power accountable.

The danger comes when we begin treating information like a menu—accepting facts from people we like and dismissing them from people we don’t.

We don’t build an informed society by hearing only voices that confirm what we already believe.

The test of a free press isn’t whether journalists tell us what we want to hear. It’s whether they are free to report facts that challenge us, our political tribe, or those in power.

A democracy requires voters.

A democracy requires elections.

A democracy requires an informed public.

And an informed public requires journalism.

Source: Scott Pelley interview with Lulu Garcia-Navarro, The New York Times.
